claim: CaRuby-Nano is a new functionalizable red calcium indicator with nanomolar affinity.
source: The great demand for long-wavelength and high signal-to-noise Ca2+ indicators has led us to develop CaRuby-Nano, a new functionalizable red calcium indicator with nanomolar affinity for use in cell biology and neuroscience research.
evidence: The abstract directly states the development and key properties of CaRuby-Nano.

claim: CaRuby-Nano has a KD of 258 ± 8 nM in cuvette calibration experiments.
source: In cuvette calibration experiments CaRuby-Nano was found to have a KD of 258 ± 8 nM, with a 50-fold (±2) increase of fluorescence on binding [Ca2+] (Figure 1B–C) and a maximum quantum yield of 0.45 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: Direct measurement data from cuvette calibration experiments is provided.

claim: CaRuby-Nano shows a 50-fold increase of fluorescence on binding calcium.
source: In cuvette calibration experiments CaRuby-Nano was found to have a KD of 258 ± 8 nM, with a 50-fold (±2) increase of fluorescence on binding [Ca2+] (Figure 1B–C) and a maximum quantum yield of 0.45 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: Direct measurement data from cuvette calibration experiments is provided.

claim: CaRuby-Nano has a maximum quantum yield of 0.45.
source: In cuvette calibration experiments CaRuby-Nano was found to have a KD of 258 ± 8 nM, with a 50-fold (±2) increase of fluorescence on binding [Ca2+] (Figure 1B–C) and a maximum quantum yield of 0.45 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: Direct measurement data from cuvette calibration experiments is provided.

claim: CaRuby-Nano exhibits effective two-photon excitation over a large wavelength band.
source: In addition to being suitable for single photon excitation, CaRuby-Nano also exhibits effective two-photon excitation over a large wavelength band (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The text states this property and references supporting figure data.

claim: Conjugation of CaRuby-Nano with dextran had only a small effect on the affinity of the indicator.
source: As expected, this conjugation had only a small effect on the affinity of the indicator, increasing the KD from 258 nM in the free salt to 295 nM in the 6 kD dextran conjugate (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Direct comparison of KD values before and after conjugation is provided.

claim: The KD of CaRuby-Nano increased from 258 nM in the free salt to 295 nM in the 6 kD dextran conjugate.
source: As expected, this conjugation had only a small effect on the affinity of the indicator, increasing the KD from 258 nM in the free salt to 295 nM in the 6 kD dextran conjugate (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Direct measurement data comparing free and conjugated forms is provided.

claim: The rising phase time course of CaRuby-Nano (0.55 ms ± 0.13 ms) was not significantly different from that found for Fluo-5F (0.40 ± 0.09 ms) under the same conditions.
source: The rising phase time course (0.55 ms ± 0.13 ms; sigmoidal fit; n = 59 spines from 7 cells) was not significantly different from that found for Fluo-5F (0.40 ± 0.09 ms, n = 36 spines from 4 cells, p = 0.37) under the same conditions, suggesting that CaRuby-Nano has binding kinetics comparable to established small molecule Ca2+ indicators.
evidence: Statistical comparison of measured time courses with p-value is provided.

claim: CaRuby-Nano has binding kinetics comparable to established small molecule Ca2+ indicators.
source: The rising phase time course (0.55 ms ± 0.13 ms; sigmoidal fit; n = 59 spines from 7 cells) was not significantly different from that found for Fluo-5F (0.40 ± 0.09 ms, n = 36 spines from 4 cells, p = 0.37) under the same conditions, suggesting that CaRuby-Nano has binding kinetics comparable to established small molecule Ca2+ indicators.
evidence: Inference is drawn from the statistical comparison of kinetics data.

claim: Single spikes resulted in reliable, easily detected fluorescence transients using CaRuby-Nano (mean dR/R0 = 0.52 ± 0.19, n = 6 cells).
source: We found that using CaRuby-Nano (6 kD dextran) even single spikes resulted in reliable, easily detected fluorescence transients (mean dR/R0 = 0.52 ± 0.19, n = 6 cells; Figure 2B).
evidence: Direct measurement data from in vivo experiments is provided.

claim: For increasing spike numbers the dR/R0 vs spike number relation quickly turns sublinear and saturates as expected for high affinity indicators.
source: For increasing spike numbers the dR/R0 vs spike number relation quickly turns sublinear and saturates as expected for high affinity indicators (Figure 2C).
evidence: Observed behavior is compared to expected behavior based on established knowledge.

claim: CaRuby-Nano is a calcium indicator with a signal quality comparable to previously used high-affinity green emitting probes.
source: Taken together these experiments demonstrate that CaRuby-Nano is a calcium indicator with a signal quality comparable to previously used high-affinity green emitting probes.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from multiple experimental comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: CaRuby-Nano is well suited for the detection of small [Ca2+] transients.
source: Importantly, it is well suited for the detection of small [Ca2+] transients, setting it apart from the previous CaRuby versions.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing detection of single spikes and small transients.

claim: Labeling with CaRuby-Nano AM in vivo was identical to that commonly found in experiments using Oregon Green-488 BAPTA-1 AM (OGB-1 AM).
source: In all cases we found labeling identical to that commonly found in experiments using Oregon Green-488 BAPTA-1 AM (OGB-1 AM) to load cerebellar tissue in vivo (Figure 3B) (Sullivan et al., 2005; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to published results using OGB-1 AM is made.

claim: Fluorescence traces from Purkinje cell dendrites loaded with CaRuby-Nano AM showed clear complex spike activity with a good signal-to-noise ratio.
source: In all experiments fluorescence traces extracted from identified Purkinje cell dendrites (Figure 3C) showed clear complex spike activity with a good signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: Direct observation from experimental data is reported.

claim: Both spontaneous activity and sensory evoked responses detected with CaRuby-Nano AM were comparable to signals detected in experiments using OGB-1 AM.
source: Both spontaneous activity and sensory evoked responses were again comparable to signals detected in experiments using OGB-1 AM (Sullivan et al., 2005; Ozden et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to published results using OGB-1 AM is made.

claim: CaRuby-Nano AM is a powerful addition to the optophysiological toolbox.
source: These results indicate that CaRuby-Nano AM is a powerful addition to the optophysiological toolbox.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from successful in vivo bulk loading experiments.

claim: CaRuby-Nano has strong two-photon excitation spectral overlap with eGFP.
source: To demonstrate the full power of CaRuby-Nano, we made use of the strong two-photon excitation spectral overlap with eGFP to conduct a set of experiments which were not possible previously: simultaneous imaging of glutamate release onto Purkinje cells using iGluSnFR (a single-wavelength extracellular glutamate indicator constructed from the bacterial glutamate sensor Gltl and circularly permutated GFP [Marvin et al., 2013]) and the resulting post-synaptic [Ca2+] increase (using CaRuby-Nano).
evidence: The property is stated and demonstrated through dual-color imaging experiments.

claim: Activation of the glutamatergic climbing fiber input evoked clear fluorescence transients in both iGluSnFR and CaRuby-Nano channels.
source: Activation of the glutamatergic climbing fiber input evoked clear fluorescence transients in both color channels (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct observation from dual-color imaging experiments is reported.

claim: Glutamate signals were confined to distinct subsections of the dendritic tree, whereas the resulting [Ca2+] transients were global.
source: Glutamate signals were confined to distinct subsections of the dendritic tree (i.e., limited to sites of synaptic glutamate release), whereas the resulting [Ca2+] transients were global, with similar amplitudes throughout different regions of the dendritic tree (Figure 4C) (Lev-Ram et al., 1992).
evidence: Direct observation from dual-color imaging experiments is reported and compared to published results.

claim: The differential spatial distribution of the signals confirms that the two indicators can be spectrally isolated.
source: The differential spatial distribution of the signals confirms that the two indicators can be spectrally isolated.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from the observed differential spatial patterns of the two indicators.

claim: Olfactory sensory neuron terminals labeled with CaRuby-Nano filled the inner glomerular boundaries.
source: Olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) terminals, labeled with CaRuby-Nano, filled the inner glomerular boundaries (Figure 4E).
evidence: Direct observation from in vivo imaging experiments is reported.

claim: Presynaptic calcium responses in single glomeruli could be recorded with excellent signal to noise ratio using CaRuby-Nano.
source: In single glomeruli (n = 8 animals) we could record presynaptic calcium responses with excellent signal to noise ratio.
evidence: Direct observation from in vivo imaging experiments is reported.

claim: Presynaptic calcium responses were selectively evoked by odor presentation in a subset of glomeruli.
source: Figure 4F shows a typical example in which presynaptic calcium responses were selectively evoked by odor presentation in a subset of glomeruli.
evidence: Direct observation from in vivo imaging experiments is reported.

claim: Presynaptic calcium responses adapted strongly at high odorant concentration, as reported previously.
source: These responses adapted strongly at this high odorant concentration, as reported previously (Lecoq et al., 2009).
evidence: Observation is consistent with previously published results.

claim: CaRuby-Nano is only slightly higher affinity than the commonly used green emitting indicator Fluo-4 (335 nM).
source: This novel indicator, CaRuby-Nano, has a KD of 295 nM (for the dextran conjugate). This makes CaRuby-Nano only slightly higher affinity than the commonly used green emitting indicator Fluo-4 (335 nM).
evidence: Direct comparison of KD values is provided.

claim: The quantum efficiency of calcium bound CaRuby-Nano (0.45) is lower than that of OGB-1 (∼0.7) but significantly higher than that of Fluo-4 (∼0.14).
source: The quantum efficiency of calcium bound CaRuby-Nano (0.45) is lower than that of OGB-1 (∼0.7) but significantly higher than that of Fluo-4 (∼0.14).
evidence: Direct comparison of quantum efficiency values is provided.

claim: CaRuby-Nano is an ideal indicator for the quantification of small intracellular [Ca2+] transients.
source: These values classify CaRuby-Nano as an ideal indicator for the quantification of small intracellular [Ca2+] transients (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from the measured properties of the indicator.

claim: CaRuby-Nano is well suited for both in vitro and in vivo imaging experiments requiring high sensitivity to [Ca2+] changes.
source: Using a range of different experiments we have demonstrated that CaRuby-Nano is well suited for both in vitro and in vivo imaging experiments requiring high sensitivity to [Ca2+] changes.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from multiple experimental demonstrations.

claim: CaRuby-Nano can be combined with activity indicators emitting in the green-yellow spectral band to allow multiplexed imaging.
source: Finally, we show that CaRuby-Nano can be combined with activity indicators emitting in the green-yellow spectral band, to allow multiplexed imaging.
evidence: Demonstrated through dual-color imaging experiments with iGluSnFR and eYFP.

claim: The azido function of CaRuby-Nano can easily be reduced to an amine group, opening the field to functionalization with numerous molecular tools.
source: The versatility of the probe is further increased by the azido function, which can easily be reduced to an amine group, thus opening the field to functionalization with numerous molecular tools such as antibodies, benzylguanine (SNAP tag) or peptides to facilitate specific sub-cellular targeting.
evidence: Chemical property and potential applications are stated based on the structure.

claim: CaRuby-Nano's sensitivity and potential for spectral multiplexing allows sophisticated experiments such as simultaneously measuring pre- and postsynaptic activity.
source: CaRuby-Nano's sensitivity and potential for spectral multiplexing allows sophisticated experiments such as simultaneously measuring pre- and postsynaptic activity or imaging of different signaling modalities in the same cell, allowing previously elusive questions to be directly addressed.
evidence: Conclusion is drawn from demonstrated properties and experiments.

claim: Red-shifted fluorophores are significantly more lipophilic than fluorescein-like dyes.
source: A major problem of red-shifted fluorophores is that they are significantly more lipophilic than fluorescein-like dyes.
evidence: General property of red-shifted fluorophores is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: Lipophilicity of red-shifted fluorophores leads to more leakage through cell membranes as well as to intracellular compartmentalization.
source: This leads to more leakage through cell membranes as well as to intracellular compartmentalization.
evidence: Consequence of lipophilicity is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: Effects of lipophilicity can be minimized by using the probes as conjugates of inert hydrophilic compounds such as dextrans.
source: These effects can be minimized by using the probes as conjugates of inert hydrophilic compounds such as dextrans.
evidence: Strategy to address lipophilicity is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: Conjugation commonly uses one of the carboxylic groups of the BAPTA moiety, affecting the calcium affinity of BAPTA-based indicators.
source: This conjugation commonly uses one of the carboxylic groups of the BAPTA moiety, affecting the calcium affinity of BAPTA-based indicators (Tsien, 1980).
evidence: Common practice and its consequence are stated with citation.

claim: Indicator-dextran conjugates are strongly shifted to lower affinities making them all but useless for sensitive and quantitative [Ca2+] measurements.
source: Consequently, these indicator-dextran conjugates are strongly shifted to lower affinities making them all but useless for sensitive and quantitative [Ca2+] measurements.
evidence: Consequence of traditional conjugation approach is stated.

claim: Lower affinity cannot be compensated for by increasing the concentration of the probe without increasing calcium buffering capacity disproportionally.
source: Importantly, this lower affinity cannot be compensated for by increasing the concentration of the probe. Such a strategy would lead to a disproportionally large increase in the calcium buffering capacity of the indicator (Neher, 2005), resulting in a stronger disruption of cellular signaling than for a low concentration of high affinity indicator (Markram et al., 1998).
evidence: Limitation of compensation strategy is explained with citations.

claim: Calcium Ruby (CaRuby) is a family of red emitting calcium indicators based on X-Rhodamine.
source: We recently introduced a family of red emitting calcium indicators based on X-Rhodamine: Calcium Ruby (CaRuby) (Collot et al., 2012), which bears an azido side arm for click chemistry and the resulting potential for high-yield coupling reactions (Kolb et al., 2001).
evidence: Previous work by the authors is described with citation.

claim: CaRuby bears an azido side arm for click chemistry and the resulting potential for high-yield coupling reactions.
source: We recently introduced a family of red emitting calcium indicators based on X-Rhodamine: Calcium Ruby (CaRuby) (Collot et al., 2012), which bears an azido side arm for click chemistry and the resulting potential for high-yield coupling reactions (Kolb et al., 2001).
evidence: Structural feature and its application are described with citations.

claim: The azido side arm efficiently allows conjugation reactions without significant perturbation of the calcium binding affinity.
source: This side arm efficiently allows conjugation reactions without significant perturbation of the calcium binding affinity (Zamaleeva et al., 2014).
evidence: Property of the azido side arm is stated with citation.

claim: The dissociation constants of CaRubies ranged from 3.4 to 21.6 µM.
source: The dissociation constants of CaRubies ranged from 3.4 to 21.6 µM—too high for the reliable detection of small [Ca2+] transients in biological tissue (Yasuda et al., 2004) (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: Properties of previous CaRuby versions are stated with citation.

claim: The dissociation constants of previous CaRubies were too high for the reliable detection of small [Ca2+] transients in biological tissue.
source: The dissociation constants of CaRubies ranged from 3.4 to 21.6 µM—too high for the reliable detection of small [Ca2+] transients in biological tissue (Yasuda et al., 2004) (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: Limitation of previous CaRuby versions is stated with citation.

claim: Increasing the electron density of BAPTA lowers its KD for calcium.
source: To increase the affinity of CaRuby, we modified the structure of the probe (Figure 1A), focusing on the Ca2+ chelating BAPTA moiety, as increasing the electron density of BAPTA lowers its KD for calcium (Tsien, 1980).
evidence: Design principle is stated with citation.

claim: An oxygen atom was introduced on one of the aromatic rings of BAPTA by a SNAr reaction.
source: We introduced an oxygen atom on one of the aromatic rings of BAPTA by a SNAr reaction.
evidence: Synthetic modification is described.

claim: The oxygen atom serves as a link for the azido side arm, which was repositioned in the new CaRuby variant.
source: This oxygen also serves as a link for the azido side arm, which was repositioned in the new CaRuby variant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural feature and its function are described.

claim: The fluorophore has an affinity-lowering effect due to its electron withdrawing nature when placed para to the nitrogen of the BAPTA.
source: Additionally, the fluorophore, which is commonly placed para to the nitrogen of the BAPTA, has an affinity-lowering effect due to its electron withdrawing nature and was therefore placed at a meta position in order to reduce its effect on the ligating nitrogen.
evidence: Design rationale based on chemical principles is explained.

claim: The fluorophore was placed at a meta position in CaRuby-Nano to reduce its effect on the ligating nitrogen.
source: Additionally, the fluorophore, which is commonly placed para to the nitrogen of the BAPTA, has an affinity-lowering effect due to its electron withdrawing nature and was therefore placed at a meta position in order to reduce its effect on the ligating nitrogen.
evidence: Design modification is described with rationale.

claim: The modifications resulted in a CaRuby variant with sub-micromolar affinity.
source: These modifications resulted in a CaRuby variant with sub-micromolar affinity ('CaRuby-Nano').
evidence: Outcome of structural modifications is stated.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation evoked calcium signals were recorded from multiple spines at acquisition rates between 2.2 and 5.0 kHz.
source: Climbing fiber stimulation evoked calcium signals were recorded from multiple spines (range: 4 to 14) at acquisition rates between 2.2 and 5.0 kHz (Figure 1E,F) using random access two-photon microscopy (Otsu et al., 2008).
evidence: Experimental parameters are reported.

claim: Fast kinetics of CaRuby-Nano point to a high sensitivity for small and fast changes in [Ca2+], such as neuronal action potentials.
source: These fast kinetics point to a high sensitivity of CaRuby-Nano for small and fast changes in [Ca2+], such as neuronal action potentials (Otsu et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference is drawn from measured kinetics with citation.

claim: Fluorescence imaging has been one of the fastest growing methods in physiology, cell biology and neuroscience in recent years.
source: In recent years fluorescence imaging has been one of the fastest growing methods in physiology, cell biology and neuroscience, constantly driving the need for improved fluorescent probes (Wilt et al., 2009; Miyawaki, 2011; Looger and Griesbeck, 2012).
evidence: General trend in the field is stated with citations.

claim: The dominance of fluorescein and eGFP in the design of probes has resulted in an overcrowding of the green spectral band.
source: The dominance of fluorescein and eGFP in the design of such probes has resulted in an overcrowding of the green spectral band.
evidence: Problem in the field is stated based on general knowledge.

claim: Overcrowding of the green spectral band makes simultaneous imaging of spatially overlapping signals problematic and emphasizes the need for red-shifted probes.
source: This makes simultaneous imaging of spatially overlapping signals problematic and emphasizes the need for red-shifted probes (Oheim et al., 2014).
evidence: Consequence and need are stated with citation.

claim: Many of the very favorable photophysical properties of fluorescein and eGFP are shared by the X-Rhodamine chromophore.
source: Many of the very favorable photophysical properties of fluorescein and eGFP are shared by the X-Rhodamine chromophore, which is finding increasing use in the development of Ca2+-indicators (Eberhard and Erne, 1991; Egawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Property comparison is stated with citations.

claim: X-Rhodamine chromophore is finding increasing use in the development of Ca2+-indicators.
source: Many of the very favorable photophysical properties of fluorescein and eGFP are shared by the X-Rhodamine chromophore, which is finding increasing use in the development of Ca2+-indicators (Eberhard and Erne, 1991; Egawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Trend in indicator development is stated with citations.
